title: इजरायलको राजनीतिक समिकरणमा प्यालेस्टिनी मत निर्णायक, १९ सीट किन बन्यो अछुत ?
content:
No ads found for this position काठमाडौं । इजरायलको संसदीय निर्वाचनमा प्यालेस्टिनी मतदाताको उल्लेख्य सहभागिताले राजनीतिक समीकरण बदल्ने अवस्था बने पनि प्रमुख यहुदी राजनीतिक दलहरू उनीहरूको समर्थन स्वीकार गर्न अनिच्छुक देखिएका छन्। मंगलबार सम्पन्न निर्वाचनमा इजरायलका प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको मतदान सहभागिता उल्लेख्य रूपमा बढेको छ। निर्वाचनमा योग्य प्यालेस्टिनी मतदातामध्ये करिब ८० प्रतिशतले मतदान गरेको अनुमान छ। इजरायलको कुल जनसंख्याको करिब २१ प्रतिशत हिस्सा ओगट्ने प्यालेस्टिनी समुदायको उच्च सहभागिताले संसद्मा उनीहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व गर्ने दुई प्रमुख राजनीतिक समूहलाई निर्णायक अवस्थामा पु¥याएको छ। प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको प्रतिनिधित्व गर्ने युनाइटेड अरब लिस्ट (राम) र जोइन्ट लिस्टले १२० सदस्यीय संसद्मा संयुक्त रूपमा १९ सिट प्राप्त गरेका छन्। यो संख्या सरकार गठनका लागि निर्णायक हुन सक्ने देखिएको छ। निर्वाचन परिणामअनुसार प्रधानमन्त्री बेन्जामिन नेतान्याहू नेतृत्वको लिकुडसहितको गठबन्धनले ५३ सिट प्राप्त गरेको छ। नेतान्याहूविरोधी यहुदी विपक्षी दलहरूको समूहले ४८ सिट पाएको छ। प्यालेस्टिनी दलका १९ सिट जोड्दा नेतान्याहूविरोधी पक्षसँग संसद्मा बहुमत पुग्ने अवस्था छ। तर सरकार गठनका लागि प्यालेस्टिनी दलको समर्थन आवश्यक देखिए पनि इजरायलका प्रमुख विपक्षी नेताहरू उनीहरूसँग गठबन्धन गर्न हच्किएका छन् । गाजामा इजरायलले गरेको नरसंहार र सरकारमा रहेका नेताहरूको नस्लवादी अभिव्यक्तिप्रति असन्तुष्टिका कारण प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिक ठूलो संख्यामा मतदानमा सहभागी भएको विश्लेषकहरूको भनाइ छ। तर निर्वाचनमा प्यालेस्टिनी मतदाताको उच्च सहभागितालाई स्वीकार गर्नुको सट्टा प्रधानमन्त्री नेतान्याहूको लिकुड पार्टीले त्यसलाई विदेशी हस्तक्षेपसँग जोडेको छ। ठूलो संख्यामा प्यालेस्टिनी मतदाता मतदानमा सहभागी हुनुको पछाडि विदेशी शक्तिको भूमिका रहेको हुन सक्ने भन्दै पार्टीले इजरायलको आन्तरिक सुरक्षा निकाय शिन बेटलाई अनुसन्धान गर्न आग्रह गरेको छ। लिकुडले निर्वाचन परिणामलाई इजरायलको ‘इस्लामीकरण’ गर्ने प्रयासका रूपमा समेत चित्रित गरेको छ। यसले प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको लोकतान्त्रिक अधिकार र उनीहरूको मतको वैधतामाथि प्रश्न उठाएको भन्दै आलोचना भएको छ। अलजजिरासँग कुरा गर्दै प्यालेस्टिनीबहुल बालाद पार्टीकी उम्मेदवार ओर्ली नोयले गाजामा इजरायली सरकारको व्यवहार र देशभित्र प्यालेस्टिनीमाथि बढ्दो दबाबले मतदातालाई मतदान केन्द्रसम्म पु¥याएको बताएकी छन्। उनका अनुसार अक्टोबर ७ पछि प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकले पाउँदै आएका सीमित अधिकारसमेत कमजोर हुँदै गएका छन्। उनीहरूले समान नागरिकका रूपमा प्रयोग गर्न पाउने अन्तिम अधिकारका रूपमा मतदानलाई लिएका कारण ठूलो संख्यामा सहभागी भएको उनको भनाइ छ। नोयले इजरायलमा बढ्दो अपराध, प्रहरी प्रशासनको कार्यशैली र अतिदक्षिणपन्थी राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षा मन्त्री इतामार बेन–गभिरको नेतृत्वप्रति असन्तुष्टिले पनि प्यालेस्टिनी मतदातालाई प्रभावित गरेको बताएकी छन्। नेतान्याहू सरकारलाई भ्रष्ट, अक्षम र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय रूपमा इजरायलको छवि कमजोर बनाउने सरकार भन्दै आलोचना गर्ने विपक्षी दलहरू पनि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग सत्ता साझेदारी गर्न हिच्किचाइरहेका छन्। इजरायलका पूर्वप्रधानमन्त्री नफ्ताली बेनेट र यायर लापिडले निर्वाचन परिणाम सार्वजनिक भएपछि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग एउटै सरकारमा नबस्ने स्पष्ट पारेका छन्। उनीहरू सन् २०२१–२२ मा सरकारमा रहँदा प्यालेस्टिनी दलको समर्थनमा निर्भर थिए। विपक्षी दलका अर्का नेता तथा यिसरेल बेतेनु पार्टीका अतिदक्षिणपन्थी नेता अविग्दोर लिबरम्यानले पनि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग गठबन्धन नगर्ने बताएका छन्। उनले नेतान्याहू र जोइन्ट लिस्टका नेता अहमद तिबी दुवैसँग एउटै गठबन्धनमा नबस्ने बताएका छन्। वामपन्थी डेमोक्रेट पार्टी भने प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग सहकार्य गर्न तुलनात्मक रूपमा इच्छुक देखिएको छ। तर विपक्षी गठबन्धनका अन्य नेताहरूले त्यसलाई अस्वीकार गरेका छन् । राजनीतिक विश्लेषक निमरोद फ्लासेनबर्गका अनुसार इजरायलको मूलधारको राजनीतिमा यहुदी सर्वोच्चताको मान्यता हावी भएकाले प्यालेस्टिनी मतलाई चुनौतीका रूपमा हेरिएको हो। सन् २०१८ मा पारित इजरायलको ‘नेसन स्टेट कानुन’ले राष्ट्रिय आत्मनिर्णयको अधिकार यहुदी जनतामा मात्र निहित हुने व्यवस्था गरेको थियो। यसले प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको समान राष्ट्रिय तथा नागरिक अधिकारसम्बन्धी माग र यहुदी राष्ट्रको अवधारणाबीचको आधारभूत राजनीतिक मतभेदलाई थप प्रस्ट पारेको विश्लेषकहरूको भनाइ छ। फ्लासेनबर्गका अनुसार इजरायलमा नागरिक हुनुको अर्थ, देश कसरी सञ्चालन हुने र राज्य कसको हितमा काम गर्ने भन्ने विषयमा यहुदी मूलधारका राजनीतिक दल र प्यालेस्टिनी समुदायबीच फरक दृष्टिकोण छ। तर त्यस्ता मतभेदले राजनीतिक व्यवहारमा देखिएको नस्लवादलाई ढाक्न नसक्ने उनको टिप्पणी छ। जोइन्ट लिस्टका हिब्रु भाषाका चुनावी अभियान निर्देशक माउरिसियो लाप्चिकले पनि यहुदी आवाजलाई मात्र प्राथमिकता दिने राजनीतिक प्रवृत्तिले प्यालेस्टिनी मतको अवमूल्यन गरेको बताएका छन्। उनका अनुसार अन्य कुनै लोकतान्त्रिक मुलुकमा विपक्षी दलको बहुमत पुग्ने अवस्था बनेमा त्यसलाई निर्वाचनमा प्राप्त जनादेशका रूपमा स्वीकार गरिन्थ्यो। तर इजरायलमा प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको मतलाई यहुदी नागरिकको मतसरह नमान्ने प्रवृत्तिका कारण उनीहरूको समर्थनबाट बनेको बहुमतलाई समेत राजनीतिक विजयका रूपमा स्वीकार गर्न कठिन भइरहेको छ। निर्वाचन परिणामले इजरायलको आगामी सरकार गठनमा प्यालेस्टिनी दल निर्णायक बन्न सक्ने देखाएको छ। तर उनीहरूको मतबाट बहुमत पुग्ने अवस्था हुँदाहुँदै पनि प्रमुख यहुदी राजनीतिक दलहरू सत्ता साझेदारी गर्न तयार नहुनुले इजरायली लोकतन्त्रमा समान राजनीतिक प्रतिनिधित्व र प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको अधिकारसम्बन्धी बहसलाई फेरि सतहमा ल्याएको छ। Kathmandu. Even as the significant participation of Palestinian voters in Israel's parliamentary elections changes the political equation, major Jewish political parties have been reluctant to accept their support. Voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel increased significantly in Tuesday's elections, with an estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters casting their ballots. The high participation of the Palestinian community, which makes up about 21 percent of Israel's total population, has put the two major political groups that represent them in parliament in a decisive position. The United Arab List (RAM) and the Joint List, which represent Palestinian citizens, have won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament. This number is seen as potentially decisive for forming a government. According to the election results, the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including Likud, won 53 seats. The group of Jewish opposition parties against Netanyahu won 48 seats. Adding the 19 seats of the Palestinian parties, the anti-Netanyahu faction is on track to achieve a majority in parliament. But even though the support of Palestinian parties appears essential to forming a government, Israel's main opposition leaders have been hesitant to form an alliance with them. Analysts say that Palestinian citizens participated in large numbers in the vote due to dissatisfaction with the massacre committed by Israel in Gaza and racist statements by leaders in the government. But instead of acknowledging the high turnout of Palestinian voters in the election, Prime Minister Netanyahu's Likud party has linked it to foreign interference. The party has called on Israel's internal security agency, the Shin Bet, to investigate, saying that foreign powers may have played a role in the large number of Palestinian voters participating in the vote. Likud has also portrayed the election results as an attempt to "Islamize" Israel, which has been criticized for questioning the democratic rights of Palestinian citizens and the legitimacy of their vote. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Orly Noy, a candidate for the predominantly Palestinian Balad party, said the Israeli government's behavior in Gaza and the increasing pressure on Palestinians inside the country were driving voters to the polls. According to him, even the limited rights enjoyed by Palestinian citizens have been eroded since October 7. He says that they participated in large numbers because they see voting as the last right they can exercise as equal citizens. Noy said rising crime in Israel, dissatisfaction with the police administration and the leadership of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gavir also influenced Palestinian voters. Opposition parties, which have criticized the Netanyahu government as corrupt, incompetent, and a government that is weakening Israel's image internationally, are also hesitant to share power with the Palestinian party. Former Israeli Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid have made it clear that they will not form a government with the Palestinian party after the election results were announced. They relied on the support of the Palestinian party when they were in government in 2021-22. Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader and leader of the far-right Yisrael Beitenu party, has also said he will not form a coalition with the Palestinian party. He said he would not sit in the same coalition with either Netanyahu or Joint List leader Ahmed Tibi. The left-wing Democratic Party has appeared relatively willing to cooperate with the Palestinian party, but other leaders in the opposition coalition have rejected it. According to political analyst Nimrod Flassenberg, the Palestinian vote is seen as a challenge because the belief in Jewish supremacy dominates mainstream Israeli politics. Israel's 'Nation State Law', passed in 2018, stipulated that the right to national self-determination was vested solely in the Jewish people. Analysts say this has further highlighted the fundamental political differences between Palestinian demands for equal national and civil rights and the concept of a Jewish state. According to Flassenberg, there are differences in views between mainstream Jewish political parties and the Palestinian community on what it means to be a citizen of Israel, how the country should be run, and whose interests the state should serve. But such differences, he notes, cannot mask the racism evident in political practice. Mauricio Lapchik, the Hebrew-language campaign director for the Joint List, also said that the political trend of prioritizing only the Jewish voice has devalued the Palestinian vote. According to him, in any other democratic country, if the opposition party achieved a majority, it would be accepted as a mandate obtained in the election. However, in Israel, due to the tendency to not consider the votes of Palestinian citizens as the same as the votes of Jewish citizens, it is becoming difficult to accept even a majority formed with their support as a political victory. The election results suggest that Palestinian parties could be decisive in forming Israel's next government. But the unwillingness of the major Jewish political parties to share power, despite their near-majority vote, has reignited the debate over equal political representation and the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israeli democracy.

Even as the significant participation of Palestinian voters in Israel's parliamentary elections changes the political equation, major Jewish political parties have been reluctant to accept their support. Voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel increased significantly in Tuesday's elections, with an estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters casting their ballots. The high participation of the Palestinian community, which makes up about 21 percent of Israel's total population, has put the two major political groups that represent them in parliament in a decisive position. The United Arab List (RAM) and the Joint List, which represent Palestinian citizens, have won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament. This number is seen as potentially decisive for forming a government. According to the election results, the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including Likud, won 53 seats. The group of Jewish opposition parties against Netanyahu won 48 seats. Adding the 19 seats of the Palestinian parties, the anti-Netanyahu faction is on track to achieve a majority in parliament. But even though the support of Palestinian parties appears essential to forming a government, Israel's main opposition leaders have been hesitant to form an alliance with them. Analysts say that Palestinian citizens participated in large numbers in the vote due to dissatisfaction with the massacre committed by Israel in Gaza and racist statements by leaders in the government. But instead of acknowledging the high turnout of Palestinian voters in the election, Prime Minister Netanyahu's Likud party has linked it to foreign interference. The party has called on Israel's internal security agency, the Shin Bet, to investigate, saying that foreign powers may have played a role in the large number of Palestinian voters participating in the vote. Likud has also portrayed the election results as an attempt to "Islamize" Israel, which has been criticized for questioning the democratic rights of Palestinian citizens and the legitimacy of their vote. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Orly Noy, a candidate for the predominantly Palestinian Balad party, said the Israeli government's behavior in Gaza and the increasing pressure on Palestinians inside the country were driving voters to the polls. According to him, even the limited rights enjoyed by Palestinian citizens have been eroded since October 7. He says that they participated in large numbers because they see voting as the last right they can exercise as equal citizens. Noy said rising crime in Israel, dissatisfaction with the police administration and the leadership of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gavir also influenced Palestinian voters. Opposition parties, which have criticized the Netanyahu government as corrupt, incompetent, and a government that is weakening Israel's image internationally, are also hesitant to share power with the Palestinian party. Former Israeli Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid have made it clear that they will not form a government with the Palestinian party after the election results were announced. They relied on the support of the Palestinian party when they were in government in 2021-22. Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader and leader of the far-right Yisrael Beitenu party, has also said he will not form a coalition with the Palestinian party. He said he would not sit in the same coalition with either Netanyahu or Joint List leader Ahmed Tibi. The left-wing Democratic Party has appeared relatively willing to cooperate with the Palestinian party, but other leaders in the opposition coalition have rejected it. According to political analyst Nimrod Flassenberg, the Palestinian vote is seen as a challenge because the belief in Jewish supremacy dominates mainstream Israeli politics. Israel's 'Nation State Law', passed in 2018, stipulated that the right to national self-determination was vested solely in the Jewish people. Analysts say this has further highlighted the fundamental political differences between Palestinian demands for equal national and civil rights and the concept of a Jewish state. According to Flassenberg, there are differences in views between mainstream Jewish political parties and the Palestinian community on what it means to be a citizen of Israel, how the country should be run, and whose interests the state should serve. But such differences, he notes, cannot mask the racism evident in political practice. Mauricio Lapchik, the Hebrew-language campaign director for the Joint List, also said that the political trend of prioritizing only the Jewish voice has devalued the Palestinian vote. According to him, in any other democratic country, if the opposition party achieved a majority, it would be accepted as a mandate obtained in the election. However, in Israel, due to the tendency to not consider the votes of Palestinian citizens as the same as the votes of Jewish citizens, it is becoming difficult to accept even a majority formed with their support as a political victory. The election results suggest that Palestinian parties could be decisive in forming Israel's next government. But the unwillingness of the major Jewish political parties to share power, despite their near-majority vote, has reignited the debate over equal political representation and the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israeli democracy.

Even as the significant participation of Palestinian voters in Israel's parliamentary elections changes the political equation, major Jewish political parties have been reluctant to accept their support. Voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel increased significantly in Tuesday's elections, with an estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters casting their ballots. The high participation of the Palestinian community, which makes up about 21 percent of Israel's total population, has put the two major political groups that represent them in parliament in a decisive position. The United Arab List (RAM) and the Joint List, which represent Palestinian citizens, have won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament. This number is seen as potentially decisive for forming a government. According to the election results, the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including Likud, won 53 seats. The group of Jewish opposition parties against Netanyahu won 48 seats. Adding the 19 seats of the Palestinian parties, the anti-Netanyahu faction is on track to achieve a majority in parliament. But even though the support of Palestinian parties appears essential to forming a government, Israel's main opposition leaders have been hesitant to form an alliance with them. Analysts say that Palestinian citizens participated in large numbers in the vote due to dissatisfaction with the massacre committed by Israel in Gaza and racist statements by leaders in the government. But instead of acknowledging the high turnout of Palestinian voters in the election, Prime Minister Netanyahu's Likud party has linked it to foreign interference. The party has called on Israel's internal security agency, the Shin Bet, to investigate, saying that foreign powers may have played a role in the large number of Palestinian voters participating in the vote. Likud has also portrayed the election results as an attempt to "Islamize" Israel, which has been criticized for questioning the democratic rights of Palestinian citizens and the legitimacy of their vote. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Orly Noy, a candidate for the predominantly Palestinian Balad party, said the Israeli government's behavior in Gaza and the increasing pressure on Palestinians inside the country were driving voters to the polls. According to him, even the limited rights enjoyed by Palestinian citizens have been eroded since October 7. He says that they participated in large numbers because they see voting as the last right they can exercise as equal citizens. Noy said rising crime in Israel, dissatisfaction with the police administration and the leadership of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gavir also influenced Palestinian voters. Opposition parties, which have criticized the Netanyahu government as corrupt, incompetent, and a government that is weakening Israel's image internationally, are also hesitant to share power with the Palestinian party. They relied on the support of the Palestinian party when they were in government in 2021-22. However, in Israel, due to the tendency to not consider the votes of Palestinian citizens as the same as the votes of Jewish citizens, it is becoming difficult to accept even a majority formed with their support as a political victory. The election results suggest that Palestinian parties could be decisive in forming Israel's next government. But the unwillingness of the major Jewish political parties to share power, despite their near-majority vote, has reignited the debate over equal political representation and the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israeli democracy.

नेतान्याहू सरकारलाई भ्रष्ट, अक्षम र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय रूपमा इजरायलको छवि कमजोर बनाउने सरकार भन्दै आलोचना गर्ने विपक्षी दलहरू पनि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग सत्ता साझेदारी गर्न हिच्किचाइरहेका छन्।

इजरायलका पूर्वप्रधानमन्त्री नफ्ताली बेनेट र यायर लापिडले निर्वाचन परिणाम सार्वजनिक भएपछि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग एउटै सरकारमा नबस्ने स्पष्ट पारेका छन्। उनीहरू सन् २०२१–२२ मा सरकारमा रहँदा प्यालेस्टिनी दलको समर्थनमा निर्भर थिए।

विपक्षी दलका अर्का नेता तथा यिसरेल बेतेनु पार्टीका अतिदक्षिणपन्थी नेता अविग्दोर लिबरम्यानले पनि प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग गठबन्धन नगर्ने बताएका छन्। उनले नेतान्याहू र जोइन्ट लिस्टका नेता अहमद तिबी दुवैसँग एउटै गठबन्धनमा नबस्ने बताएका छन्।

वामपन्थी डेमोक्रेट पार्टी भने प्यालेस्टिनी दलसँग सहकार्य गर्न तुलनात्मक रूपमा इच्छुक देखिएको छ। तर विपक्षी गठबन्धनका अन्य नेताहरूले त्यसलाई अस्वीकार गरेका छन् ।

राजनीतिक विश्लेषक निमरोद फ्लासेनबर्गका अनुसार इजरायलको मूलधारको राजनीतिमा यहुदी सर्वोच्चताको मान्यता हावी भएकाले प्यालेस्टिनी मतलाई चुनौतीका रूपमा हेरिएको हो।

सन् २०१८ मा पारित इजरायलको ‘नेसन स्टेट कानुन’ले राष्ट्रिय आत्मनिर्णयको अधिकार यहुदी जनतामा मात्र निहित हुने व्यवस्था गरेको थियो। यसले प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको समान राष्ट्रिय तथा नागरिक अधिकारसम्बन्धी माग र यहुदी राष्ट्रको अवधारणाबीचको आधारभूत राजनीतिक मतभेदलाई थप प्रस्ट पारेको विश्लेषकहरूको भनाइ छ।

फ्लासेनबर्गका अनुसार इजरायलमा नागरिक हुनुको अर्थ, देश कसरी सञ्चालन हुने र राज्य कसको हितमा काम गर्ने भन्ने विषयमा यहुदी मूलधारका राजनीतिक दल र प्यालेस्टिनी समुदायबीच फरक दृष्टिकोण छ। तर त्यस्ता मतभेदले राजनीतिक व्यवहारमा देखिएको नस्लवादलाई ढाक्न नसक्ने उनको टिप्पणी छ।

जोइन्ट लिस्टका हिब्रु भाषाका चुनावी अभियान निर्देशक माउरिसियो लाप्चिकले पनि यहुदी आवाजलाई मात्र प्राथमिकता दिने राजनीतिक प्रवृत्तिले प्यालेस्टिनी मतको अवमूल्यन गरेको बताएका छन्।

उनका अनुसार अन्य कुनै लोकतान्त्रिक मुलुकमा विपक्षी दलको बहुमत पुग्ने अवस्था बनेमा त्यसलाई निर्वाचनमा प्राप्त जनादेशका रूपमा स्वीकार गरिन्थ्यो। तर इजरायलमा प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको मतलाई यहुदी नागरिकको मतसरह नमान्ने प्रवृत्तिका कारण उनीहरूको समर्थनबाट बनेको बहुमतलाई समेत राजनीतिक विजयका रूपमा स्वीकार गर्न कठिन भइरहेको छ।

निर्वाचन परिणामले इजरायलको आगामी सरकार गठनमा प्यालेस्टिनी दल निर्णायक बन्न सक्ने देखाएको छ। तर उनीहरूको मतबाट बहुमत पुग्ने अवस्था हुँदाहुँदै पनि प्रमुख यहुदी राजनीतिक दलहरू सत्ता साझेदारी गर्न तयार नहुनुले इजरायली लोकतन्त्रमा समान राजनीतिक प्रतिनिधित्व र प्यालेस्टिनी नागरिकको अधिकारसम्बन्धी बहसलाई फेरि सतहमा ल्याएको छ।

Even as the significant participation of Palestinian voters in Israel's parliamentary elections changes the political equation, major Jewish political parties have been reluctant to accept their support. Voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel increased significantly in Tuesday's elections, with an estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters casting their ballots. The high participation of the Palestinian community, which makes up about 21 percent of Israel's total population, has put the two major political groups that represent them in parliament in a decisive position. The United Arab List (RAM) and the Joint List, which represent Palestinian citizens, have won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament. This number is seen as potentially decisive for forming a government. According to the election results, the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including Likud, won 53 seats. The group of Jewish opposition parties against Netanyahu won 48 seats. Adding the 19 seats of the Palestinian parties, the anti-Netanyahu faction is on track to achieve a majority in parliament. But even though the support of Palestinian parties appears essential to forming a government, Israel's main opposition leaders have been hesitant to form an alliance with them. Analysts say that Palestinian citizens participated in large numbers in the vote due to dissatisfaction with the massacre committed by Israel in Gaza and racist statements by leaders in the government. But instead of acknowledging the high turnout of Palestinian voters in the election, Prime Minister Netanyahu's Likud party has linked it to foreign interference. The party has called on Israel's internal security agency, the Shin Bet, to investigate, saying that foreign powers may have played a role in the large number of Palestinian voters participating in the vote. Likud has also portrayed the election results as an attempt to "Islamize" Israel, which has been criticized for questioning the democratic rights of Palestinian citizens and the legitimacy of their vote. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Orly Noy, a candidate for the predominantly Palestinian Balad party, said the Israeli government's behavior in Gaza and the increasing pressure on Palestinians inside the country were driving voters to the polls. According to him, even the limited rights enjoyed by Palestinian citizens have been eroded since October 7. He says that they participated in large numbers because they see voting as the last right they can exercise as equal citizens. Noy said rising crime in Israel, dissatisfaction with the police administration and the leadership of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gavir also influenced Palestinian voters. Opposition parties, which have criticized the Netanyahu government as corrupt, incompetent, and a government that is weakening Israel's image internationally, are also hesitant to share power with the Palestinian party. Former Israeli Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid have made it clear that they will not form a government with the Palestinian party after the election results were announced. They relied on the support of the Palestinian party when they were in government in 2021-22. Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader and leader of the far-right Yisrael Beitenu party, has also said he will not form a coalition with the Palestinian party. He said he would not sit in the same coalition with either Netanyahu or Joint List leader Ahmed Tibi. The left-wing Democratic Party has appeared relatively willing to cooperate with the Palestinian party, but other leaders in the opposition coalition have rejected it. According to political analyst Nimrod Flassenberg, the Palestinian vote is seen as a challenge because the belief in Jewish supremacy dominates mainstream Israeli politics. Israel's 'Nation State Law', passed in 2018, stipulated that the right to national self-determination was vested solely in the Jewish people. Analysts say this has further highlighted the fundamental political differences between Palestinian demands for equal national and civil rights and the concept of a Jewish state. According to Flassenberg, there are differences in views between mainstream Jewish political parties and the Palestinian community on what it means to be a citizen of Israel, how the country should be run, and whose interests the state should serve. But such differences, he notes, cannot mask the racism evident in political practice. Mauricio Lapchik, the Hebrew-language campaign director for the Joint List, also said that the political trend of prioritizing only the Jewish voice has devalued the Palestinian vote. According to him, in any other democratic country, if the opposition party achieved a majority, it would be accepted as a mandate obtained in the election. However, in Israel, due to the tendency to not consider the votes of Palestinian citizens as the same as the votes of Jewish citizens, it is becoming difficult to accept even a majority formed with their support as a political victory. The election results suggest that Palestinian parties could be decisive in forming Israel's next government. But the unwillingness of the major Jewish political parties to share power, despite their near-majority vote, has reignited the debate over equal political representation and the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israeli democracy.
